profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-based interdisciplinary methods team is planning a short internal briefing note and reproducible demo for colleagues in economics, operations research, and energy systems on how the nucleolus of a characteristic function game can be explained using a modern applied example rather than a purely abstract theorem statement. The meeting is between the lead researcher shaping the mathematical content and the research software specialist coordinating the demo package. The agenda is to decide what the deliverable includes, how the example game will be represented, what needs to be prepared for the briefing, and who owns each piece over the next ten days. The expected outcome is a shared plan for a concise note, a demonstration artifact, assigned responsibilities, and a timeline for circulation before an internal seminar.

members.name: Dr. Mira Levin
members.expertise: cooperative game theory, allocation rules, mathematical exposition
members.background: Mira teaches graduate game theory and often translates classic papers into contemporary examples for cross-disciplinary audiences; she typically works from formal characteristic-function definitions and hand-checkable small games before anything computational is automated.
members.private_state: She wants the briefing to preserve conceptual fidelity to Schmeidler's original framing and avoid being seen as oversimplifying the nucleolus into just another fairness heuristic; she is also trying to keep the scope small enough that she can review all mathematics personally before the seminar.
hidden_assumptions: A 'demo' for an internal methods briefing means a worked 3-player or 4-player example that can be followed on a slide or whiteboard, with any code only serving as a check.
When people say 'the game specification' for a characteristic function game, they mean the coalition-value table v(S) itself, not a separate generative optimization model.
If the team says they will 'verify the result', that means checking the lexicographic excess ordering by hand or with a transparent notebook on a single final game instance.
A 'brief note' naturally includes only the nucleolus construction and final allocation for the base transferable-utility game, not robustness variants or sensitivity sweeps.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.role: Research Software Engineer for Decision Analytics
members.expertise: optimization pipelines, reproducible computational notebooks, applied energy and logistics examples
members.background: Alex supports faculty across domains by turning mathematical methods into runnable artifacts for workshops and internal showcases; he usually packages examples as parameterized notebooks with small data files and automated checks so others can reuse them later.
members.private_state: He wants the output to look reusable and polished enough to become a lab template for future allocation-method demos; he is concerned that a static toy example will be dismissed by applied colleagues unless it can be rerun on a realistic parameterized case.
hidden_assumptions: A 'demo' means a runnable notebook that takes an application dataset or parameter file and computes the nucleolus end-to-end for at least one realistic use case.
When people refer to 'the game specification', they mean the encoded model and inputs from which coalition values are generated, because that is what makes the demo reproducible.
To 'verify the result' means comparing outputs across solver runs, checking constraints programmatically, and confirming the allocation remains stable under small input perturbations.
A 'brief note' for cross-domain colleagues should include at least a small sensitivity section so readers can see the method is not tied to one arbitrary coalition table.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to prepare 'the demo' for the seminar.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 understands 'the demo' as a compact worked example of a characteristic function game, probably 3 or 4 players, shown in slides and optionally checked in a notebook.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 understands 'the demo' as a runnable notebook with inputs, code, and outputs that attendees can execute themselves on a small applied instance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In academic planning conversations, 'demo' comfortably covers both a pedagogical walkthrough and a computational artifact, so each hears a familiar and legitimate version of the same commitment.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Alex will package 'the game specification' and Mira will review it.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this package is just the final characteristic-function table listing v(S) for each coalition in the chosen example, plus notation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this package includes the parameter file, coalition-generation logic, and script that computes coalition values before the nucleolus step.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both views are standard in adjacent communities: theorists treat the characteristic function itself as the game, while software-oriented applied researchers treat the full value-generation pipeline as part of the specification.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to verify the result
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the allocation should be 'verified before circulation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes verification is complete once the excess vector ordering is transparently checked for the selected game and no mathematical inconsistency appears in the note.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes verification requires automated reproducibility checks and at least a couple of nearby parameter variations to show the notebook behaves consistently.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Verification sounds like a universally shared quality standard, but in mixed math/software teams it silently shifts between proof-oriented correctness and pipeline-oriented robustness without anyone noticing.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the brief note
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to circulate 'a brief note' ahead of the seminar.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a two-to-three-page conceptual note containing the definition of the nucleolus, one base example, and a short interpretation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the note to include a short appendix or extra section on sensitivity runs and instructions for reproducing the example from the notebook.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both still consider the document 'brief'; the disagreement is about what naturally fits inside that label, and the extra material sounds like harmless support rather than a scope change.
